newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Maluf turns up heat in Brazil re-election debate.
newsitem.headline: Maluf turns up heat in Brazil re-election debate.

text.p: Brazil's re-election debate heated up on Tuesday when Sao Paulo mayor and presidential hopeful Paulo Maluf launched a broadside against President Fernando Henrique Cardoso's dream of running again in 1998.

"The government is hostage to re-election...Nothing is being done in this country because re-election is everything," Maluf told a packed meeting of a lower house panel mulling a proposed constitutional amendment that would give presidents, state governors and mayors the chance of a second term.

Maluf told the panel he backed the concept of re-election, but only for future holders of executive office, a position which observers say would bolster his chances of winning the 1998 presidential race by sidelining the popular Cardoso.

He also said he backed the idea of a plebiscite on re-election: "You can't change the rules in the middle of the game. Either you consult the people or you approve re-election only for future presidents."

Maluf, riding high on the success of his hand-chosen successor in Sao Paulo's municipal elections earlier this month, shied away from declaring his intention to run in 1998, but treated his audience to a campaign-style promises of public works, lower unemployment and safer streets.
He was speaking in the first of several public hearings to be held by the lower house committee.

Opponents of re-election due to address the panel later this week include two respected members of Cardoso's own Brazilian Social Democratic Party (PSDB) -- Sao Paulo governor Mario Covas and former finance minister Ciro Gomes.
Despite the harsh words, observers say the government is virtually guaranteed the simple majority it needs for the proposal to be approved in the panel and advance to the floor of the lower house.
That is where the real battle is likely to take place because the government needs to two three-fifths majorities which Maluf will be doing his utmost to deny it.
